tagline: Early automobile touring links mountain parks, dinosaur fossils and a sandstone theater
intro: Lariat Loop winds through the Front Range foothills west of Denver, linking Golden, Morrison and Evergreen over 40 miles. Forests, rocky ridges, canyons and meadows give the drive its changing shape, with the five-mile Lariat Trail crossing Lookout Mountain. Colorado’s Department of Transportation lists two hours of driving and presents this National Scenic Byway as a way to revisit early automobile touring among mountain parks and heritage sites.

The mountain road was built in 1913 up Lookout Mountain’s steep eastern side. It became part of a larger touring landscape: the loop includes portions of Denver’s original circle drives in the Mountain Parks system designed by F. L. Olmsted Jr. in 1914. Tourism promotion began that same year; Colorado’s scenic-byway designation followed in 2002. Two of those drives are listed on the National Register of Historic Places: the Bear Creek Canyon Scenic Mountain Drive and the Lariat Trail Scenic Mountain Drive.

Starting in Golden, take the loop south toward Dinosaur Ridge, Red Rocks and Morrison, then follow Highway 74 through Bear Creek Canyon to Evergreen. From Evergreen the route turns north toward Interstate 70 and Genesee Park. Lookout Mountain Road and the Lariat Trail complete the circuit, descending the mountain’s eastern slope back to Golden.

moments.title: Dinosaur Ridge
moments.text: Two sides of Dinosaur Ridge hold different chapters of the fossil record. On the west, Arthur Lakes and Henry Beckwith found dinosaur material in the Morrison Formation in 1877. The first identified Stegosaurus fossils came from here. On the east, construction crews building Alameda Parkway to Red Rocks in 1937 uncovered tracks in the younger Dakota Formation. The outdoor exhibits follow a closed portion of that road, with signs explaining bones, tracks and local geology. Friends of Dinosaur Ridge formed in 1989 to address preservation concerns and provide educational programs about the site.
moments.notice: Look for rusty brown fossil bones in the quarry layer.

moments.title: Red Rocks Amphitheatre
moments.text: Ship Rock and Creation Rock flank the seating at Red Rocks, with smaller Stage Rock completing the natural amphitheater. The Fountain Formation rocks were lifted and tilted during the Laramide Orogeny; oxidized minerals give the formations their red color. John Brisben Walker developed a temporary concert platform here after buying the property in 1906. Denver later commissioned architects Burnham F. Hoyt and Stanley E. Morse, with Civilian Conservation Corps and Works Progress Administration labor and materials, to build the theater dedicated in 1941. The 9,525-capacity venue fits its seating between those sandstone formations.
moments.notice: Ship Rock, Creation Rock and smaller Stage Rock frame the theater.

moments.title: Lookout Mountain
moments.text: The road up Lookout Mountain arrived after an unsuccessful railway project. The Denver Resort Railway and Telegraph Company began its line in 1890, but never completed or opened it. The 1913 road climbed the steep eastern slope from Golden. At 7,377 feet, the summit overlooks downtown Denver, twelve miles east. William Frederick “Buffalo Bill” Cody was buried here in June 1917, the year Denver acquired part of the earlier Lookout Mountain Park. In 1921, a rustic wooden lodge called Pahaska Tepee joined the gravesite, housing the Buffalo Bill Museum and giving visitors a place to learn his story.
moments.notice: Downtown Denver is visible twelve miles east of the mountain.
